source.title: Characterising Universal Jailbreak Features and Refusal Direction in LLMs
source.authors: Canaan Yung; Hanxun Huang; Christopher Leckie; Sarah Monazam Erfani

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates cross-model similarity of derived directions and whether an averaged direction predicts transferable jailbreaks, but uses external text embeddings and classifiers rather than the original residual-stream difference-in-means and causal interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper's “universal refusal direction” is an average of per-model logistic-probe weights in concatenated SBERT prompt-embedding space. It is evaluated as a predictor of jailbreak success, not by ablating or adding a residual-stream direction. Tables 1–2 evaluate the feature space generally, not the universal direction, so they are not recorded as rows. The HarmBench judge prompt is a study evaluation script, not an instruction to the AI reviewing this paper.
record.test_reason: The 'universal refusal direction' is the normalized average of per-model logistic-probe weights. The probes are fit on external SBERT prompt embeddings (cSBERT) to predict HarmBench-judged jailbreak success. It is not a difference-in-means direction in any model's activations. Nothing is ablated, added or carried into another model's activations. The paper cites Arditi et al. to justify assuming refusal is one-dimensional ('we posit... effectively one-dimensional', §3.3). It then reports only its own detector's AUC and accuracy. Its results therefore do not bear on whether a model's internal refusal direction transfers across models, languages or base/instruct variants (V6), or on any other version. This is a related construct: a classifier direction for predicting jailbreak success in a shared embedding space.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that cSBERT is a universal feature space for predicting jailbreak success, including for black-box models. They report shared jailbreak features across LLMs via MLP-LRP. Averaging per-model probe directions gives a one-dimensional 'universal refusal direction' that detects transferable jailbreaks. They do go further than the paraphrase: they state this confirms 'modeling refusal as a linear one-dimensional direction'. That inference rests on predictive probe performance, not causal tests.
record.recipe_differences: Uses concatenated external SBERT embeddings, logistic probes, and MLP-LRP attributions; averages learned probe weights and tests predictive detection. It does not use the original residual-stream difference-in-means direction or intervene on model activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with dataset, embedding space, and classification threshold. The transfer evaluation holds out attack types; cross-model similarity is reported to vary by model pair.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-model logistic-probe weights predicting jailbreak success in concatenated SBERT space are averaged into one vector. Projection onto it detects prompts that jailbreak at least 4 of 7 models on held-out attack types: AUC 0.757 (JB10800) and 0.669 (JailbreakBench); max-F1 accuracy 0.781 and 0.799.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A shared external-embedding linear direction predicts which jailbreak prompts transfer across LLMs, including black-box models.

fits_no_version.finding: MLP-LRP attribution vectors of per-model jailbreak-success probes show mean cross-model cosine similarity near 0.5 in cSBERT versus about 0.3 in E5 and BGE. Some family pairs approach 0.7; GPT-4.1 and Mistral align less.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jailbreak-success features in a shared prompt-embedding space are partly common across LLMs.

record.problems: The measured direction is in external prompt-embedding space, and its evaluation is predictive rather than causal. Transfer tests hold out attack types rather than models. Table 3 provides no uncertainty estimates; direction-similarity values are largely described qualitatively in the text. No general-capability evaluation is reported.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row cap. Table 1–2 and Appendix C results concern general jailbreak-success prediction in feature spaces/classifiers rather than the averaged universal direction, so they are noted in gate_note rather than included.

untested.parts: No residual-stream difference-in-means direction, no ablation or addition, no capability check.
No test of jailbreaks suppressing an internal refusal direction; no adversarial training.
One-dimensionality is assumed, not compared with affine, cone or multi-direction accounts.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
No transfer of an internal refusal direction across models, languages, or base vs instruct. Similarity is measured only between external-embedding probe attributions.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all 61 rows to V6 and gave supports/limits_scope labels. Those links are dropped. The 'refusal direction' here is a detector weight vector over external sentence embeddings, so its success or failure says nothing about the internal residual-stream direction the versions name. Tables 1, 2, 6 and 7 (general jailbreak-success prediction) were correctly left out. The HarmBench judge prompt in the appendix is evaluation material and was not treated as instructions.

versions.untested_parts: No residual-stream difference-in-means direction, ablation, addition, causal mediation test, or general-capability check.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or training against its ablation.
No test comparing affine, cone, or multidirectional refusal mechanisms against a dominant direction.
No separation test of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.

Tests cross-model similarity and prediction of transferable attacks using its own external-embedding directions; does not test language transfer, base-to-instruct transfer, held-out-model transfer, or causal transfer of the original residual-stream direction.
No comparison of refusal-training methods, timing, or training stages.

rows.subject: Universal refusal direction (cSBERT; averaged across seven LLMs)
rows.size_stated: Seven-model aggregate; component models include Gemma-7B-IT, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-3B-IT, Mistral-8B-IT, Qwen-2.5-7B-IT, Claude-4-Sonnet, and GPT-4.1
rows.stage_stated: Aggregate of listed chat/instruct and proprietary models
rows.operation_detail: Project prompts onto the averaged normalized per-LLM logistic-probe direction and classify transferable jailbreaks
rows.measure: AUC for predicting transferable jailbreak prompts
rows.note: Transferable prompts are defined as jailbreaks of at least four of seven models; test attack type is held out.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: cSBERT universal direction on the two held-out-attack datasets; high-alignment model-family pairs
reader_labels.reason: The averaged direction predicts transferable jailbreak prompts at the reported cSBERT scores, and named model-family MLP-LRP directions show cosine similarity approaching 0.7 (r1–r8, r57, r60). This supports cross-model transfer in the paper's tested prompt-embedding setting, not causal transfer of a residual-stream direction.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: individual feature spaces and GPT 4.1/Mistral 8B alignment
reader_labels.reason: Direction performance varies by embedding and dataset, and the paper reports lower cross-model alignment for GPT 4.1 and Mistral 8B; testing holds out attack types, not models (r9–r56, r58, r59, r61).
